notes:
I've written notes for vv. 25–29 and v. 39, where the sources were strong. Most of vv. 30–47 is covered only by short summaries, and v. 30 has no notes at all because I didn't find a page that comments on it directly. My tool budget ran out before I could read the verse pages for v. 30 and vv. 31–47, and before I could get to netbible.org, the Catholic and Orthodox sites, or any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace material.

---

**v. 25: "the dead will hear… and live"**

*Traditional reading.* Most of these writers take "the dead" to mean the spiritually dead.
- Ellicott: the reference here, as in the whole of this paragraph (John 5:21-27), is to the spiritually dead. This is shown by the "now is," which cannot be applied to the physical resurrection. https://biblehub.com/john/5-25.htm
- Matthew Poole lists three views: the people Jesus raised during his ministry, such as Lazarus; the general resurrection; and the spiritually dead. He sides with the third: the most and best interpreters rather understand these words of those who are dead in trespasses and sins. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/5-25.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown read "now is" as the start of this hour and Pentecost as its "whole fulness." They say Jesus moves from "hearing his word" (v. 24) to "the voice of the Son of God" to signify that as it finds men in a dead condition, so it carries with it a resurrection-power. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/5-25.htm
- Barnes holds both senses. The renewal of the heart, and the raising of the dead at the judgment, are here also described in similar language, because they so far resemble each other that the same language will apply to both. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/5-25.htm
- Gill thinks the miracles of raising the dead are possible but prefers the spiritual reading, and he takes Christ's "voice" to be the gospel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/5-25.htm
- Matthew Henry separates this verse from v. 28: This is plainly distinguished from that in John 5:28, which speaks of the resurrection at the end of time. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/5-25.html

*Where Protestant traditions differ: who is able to hear?*
- **Reformed (Calvin):** he does not speak indiscriminately of all the dead, but means the elect only, whose ears God pierces and opens. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/5-25.html
- **Baptist (John MacArthur):** a similar line. This is an effectual hearing, this is a hearing in the believing heart and the believing soul, this is based upon God's gracious awakening of the dead soul. https://www.gty.org/library/sermons-library/43-28/the-dead-will-hear-christ
- **Baptist (John Piper):** he reads v. 25 alongside vv. 28–29 and stresses Jesus' power over physical death. Jesus was showing in that hour what the last hour would be like. And he was revealing more of his glory—the glory of his sovereign voice over death. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-life-giving-voice-of-the-son-of-god
- **Methodist (Adam Clarke):** he finds three meanings: the final resurrection, the people Jesus was about to raise, and the hour now is, when many who are dead in trespasses and sins, shall hear the voice (the word) of the Son of God, believe, and receive spiritual life through him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/5-25.html
- **Holiness (Godbey, 1896):** This has direct allusion to spiritual resurrection. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/net/john/5-25.html
- **Calvary Chapel (Chuck Smith):** an unusual reading that ties the verse to Christ preaching to the dead: Jesus will soon be going down into hell and preaching to those souls in prison. That He might deliver them from their captivity. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/5-25.html

*Other views.* The Lutheran commentator Meyer rejects the idea that this verse means the literal raisings, because those people were not at all awaked to ζωή in the sense of the context, but only to the earthly life, which was still liable to death. He notes that Hengstenberg and Olshausen took the literal view. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/5-25.htm

---

**v. 26: "life in Himself"**

*Traditional reading.* Biblehub's study notes: The Father is eternally self-existent; out of that fullness He grants the same self-existent life to the Son. https://biblehub.com/john/5-26.htm

*The Son "begotten" from eternity (eternal generation).*
- Augustine's answer to how the Son received this life is that the Father "begat" the Son. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/is-the-eternal-generation-of-the-son-a-biblical-idea/
- A Themelios article published by The Gospel Coalition says scholars remain divided on whether this text refers to an eternal grant of life to the Son from the Father or a grant from the time of the incarnation. It sides with the older view, quoting Chrysostom that "hath given" equals "hath begotten." https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/article/granted-life-in-himself-is-it-plausible-to-see-eternal-generation-in-john-526/
- D. A. Carson calls this verse as close as you get in the New Testament to what in the Patristic period was known as the eternal generation of the Son. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/the-spirituality-of-the-gospel-of-john-part-3-john-5/
- Gill applies the verse to the eternal life the Father has placed in Christ's hands to give to his people. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/mnt/john/5-26.html

---

**v. 27: Judge "because He is the Son of Man"**
- William Kelly: although the Son was a man, in that very position had the Father given Him to have life in Himself, and to execute judgment also, because He is Son of man. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/5-25.html
- Guzik on the wider passage: It is before God the Son that people will stand on the Day of Judgment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-5/

---

**vv. 28–29: Everyone in the graves will come out**

*Traditional reading.*
- Godbey: a clear and positive revelation, assuring us that all, both good and bad, will be raised from the dead. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/net/john/5-25.html
- Piper tells hearers that Your decomposed body will obey the voice of the Son of God. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-life-giving-voice-of-the-son-of-god

*"Those who have done good": the faith-and-works question.*
- **Reformed (Calvin):** He points out believers by good works, as he elsewhere teaches that a tree is known by its fruit. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/5-29.html
- **Dispensational (Constable):** Believers are those who do good, which involves believing on the Son (John 6:29). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/5-29.html
- **Matthew Henry** puts weight on how a person actually lived: Whatever name men are called by, or whatever plausible profession they make, it will be well in the great day with those only that have done good. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/5-29.html
- **Biblehub Q&A:** works show who truly believed but do not earn salvation: "doing good" is diagnostic, not meritorious. https://biblehub.com/q/John_5_29_vs_faith-alone_salvation.htm
- **Methodist (Wesley):** a brief note only: That resurrection which leads to life everlasting. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wes/john/5-29.html

*Other views.* Barker and Kohlenberger, as quoted in the Light of Israel commentary, note that this passage contains one of the few references to eschatology (study of last things) in John's gospel. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/5-29.html

---

**vv. 31–38: The witnesses (John the Baptist, the works, the Father)**

I could not read verse-level commentary on vv. 31–36.
- Guzik's chapter overview lists the witnesses: John the Baptist, His works, the Father Himself, Scripture, and Moses—that all testify to who He truly is. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-5/
- **v. 37:** Godbey raises the problem of the Old Testament appearances of God, asking Did not God come into the garden and speak to Adam and Eve face to face? https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/net/john/5-25.html
- **v. 38:** Matthew Henry says God's word dwells in a person when it shows in what they do, especially Christ whom he hath sent. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/5-39.html

---

**v. 39: "You pore over the Scriptures"**

This verse has a long-running grammatical debate. The Greek verb can be a statement ("you search") or a command ("search!"). Ellicott says scholarly opinion has been, and is, almost equally divided. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/5-39.htm

*Reading it as a statement ("you search").*
- Ellicott points out that the verbs around it are statements and asks: Why should there be a sudden change of construction in this instance only? https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/5-39.htm
- **Methodist (Clarke):** it should be translated, not in the imperative, but in the indicative mood-thus, Ye search the Scriptures diligently. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/5-39.html
- **Constable:** the leaders studied the Old Testament for the wrong reason, namely, to earn eternal life through their effort. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/5-39.html
- **Utley:** Since it is in a list of witnesses that the Jews had rejected it is probably an indicative. https://bible.org/book/export/html/19298
- **Coffman (Church of Christ):** Jesus is recognising how familiar they were with the Old Testament, not commanding them to study it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/5-39.html

*Reading it as a command ("search!").* Many leading Protestants took it this way, so the split is not neatly along denominational lines.
- Barnes's list of those who read it as a command: Chrysostom, Augustine, Luther, Calvin, Wetstein, Stier, Alford, and others. He concludes that both readings are legitimate. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/5-39.htm
- **Matthew Henry** keeps both. Read as a command, the verse becomes advice to all Christians to search the scriptures. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/5-39.html
- **Calvin:** the leaders perceived nothing in them but the dead letter. https://www.studylight.org/bible/kor/kor/john/5-39.html

*Catholic and early church.*
- Cornelius a Lapide (Jesuit, 1614) reports that Cyril read it as a statement, while Augustine, Chrysostom, Theophylact and Euthymius read it as a command. He urges preachers to search Scripture and they will find Christ in them all, either openly revealed, or else veiled in shadows and figures. https://www.studylight.org/bible/kor/kor/john/5-39.html
- The Golden Chain (Aquinas's collection of the Church Fathers) reads it as a command. https://www.studylight.org/bible/kor/kor/john/5-39.html

*Modern scholarship (ICC, 1895).*
- The command reading goes back to Origen and Tertullian, but the ICC prefers the statement reading. It cites a rabbinic saying that "he who has acquired the words of the Law has acquired eternal life". https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nkj/john/5-39.html

---

**vv. 40–44: Refusing to come; looking for honour from people**
- Guzik's chapter summary (marked on the page as AI-generated) says the leaders' rejection was not intellectual but spiritual: they loved the honor of men more than the honor that comes from God, and pride made faith impossible for them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-5/
- Matthew Henry (Concise): They did indeed search the Scriptures, but it was with a view to their own glory. It is possible for men to be very studious in the letter of the Scriptures, yet to be strangers to its power. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/5-39.htm

**vv. 45–47: Moses as their accuser**
- Guzik's summary: their refusal to believe Moses' writings made their rejection of Jesus's own words inevitable. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-5/

---

**Gaps to fill next:** the per-verse Biblehub commentary pages for vv. 30–47 (Gill, Ellicott, Pulpit, Wesley); netbible.org notes; the Catholic and Orthodox sites (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org); and anything on v. 43 ("another… in his own name"), which some read as pointing to false messiahs or the Antichrist.
